title: TCP and IP Bake Off
summary: Describes procedures, scoring and tests used in the TCP and IP "bake offs" held in the early development of these protocols. Those procedures and tests may still help in testing newly implemented TCP and IP modules.

plainLanguage.summary: Different teams built their own versions of the Internet's rules. A bake off was a contest where they tried them out together to see which ones worked with each other.

questions: what was the tcp ip bake off
how were early tcp implementations tested
what is the flakeway in networking tests
subtitle: Testing procedures and scoring for early TCP and IP implementations.

tldr.problem: In the early days of TCP and IP, with few implementations and evolving specifications, there was no standard way to verify that an implementation was correct.
tldr.mechanism: The solution was to hold "Bake Offs": focused testing events where all known implementations were brought together to test against each other, using a defined set of tests and scoring procedures.
tldr.outcome: These events served to both validate implementations and refine the specifications themselves. The procedures documented here remain useful as guidance for testing newly implemented TCP and IP modules.

today: RFC 1025 is an Informational document describing historical testing procedures. While the specific bake offs ended decades ago, the testing framework and procedures described here remain useful as guidance for validating newly implemented TCP and IP modules.

sections.title: Early Protocol Testing and the Bake Off Concept
sections.content:
RFC 1025 describes procedures from testing events called "Bake Offs," held in the early days of TCP and IP development. At that time, specifications were still evolving and there were only a few implementations. The only practical way to determine if an implementation was correct was to test it against other implementations and see if they worked together.

Several such testing events were organized: a demonstration of four TCP implementations in December 1978, a bake off of six implementations in January 1979 at USC-ISI, and a distributed bake off over the network in April 1980. The April 1980 event produced procedures and tests that have remained useful for validating newly implemented TCP and IP modules.
sections.plainLanguage: When the Internet was being invented, different teams each built their own version of TCP and IP. They had contests called "Bake Offs" where all the versions tried to work together, to see which ones were right.

sections.title: The Testing Framework: Three Divisions
sections.content:
The bake off testing framework was organized into four categories, with scoring that rewarded both basic capabilities and correct handling of tricky cases. The Featherweight Division tested local TCP functionality: opening a connection to yourself, sending data to yourself, gracefully closing, and repeating without reinitializing. It also tested basic operation through a test gateway.

The Middleweight Division repeated these tests but with another TCP implementation, adding connectivity tests between different systems. The Heavyweight Division tested advanced capabilities: simultaneous multiple connections, urgent data handling, sequence number wraparound, and especially the ability to handle "Kamikaze" packets—segments with many flags set at once, which would crash incorrect implementations.

Finally, the Host and Gateway IP Division tested IP features like fragmentation and reassembly, source routing options, type of service, security options, and proper handling of time-to-live fields.
sections.plainLanguage: Teams could earn points for different tricks: talking to themselves, talking to others, handling weird packets that would crash bad code, and testing the IP layer's special features.

sections.title: Test Procedures and the Flakeway
sections.content:
The RFC includes a detailed test procedure where each implementor runs a specific set of tests and reports results. Most tests were done using a test program or Telnet to open connections to other TCP implementations on the network.

An important tool described in the procedures is the flakeway: a purposely unreliable gateway that could be adjusted while running to drop datagrams at a specified percentage, corrupt and pass on a percentage of datagrams, or reorder datagrams so they arrived in a different order than sent. This allowed test of how robustly implementations handled packet loss and out-of-order delivery.

A critical requirement was that checksums must be enforced in all tests. Implementations that disabled checksum testing received no points for any checksum-related tests, even if they had implemented other features correctly.
sections.plainLanguage: Testers used a fake broken network that could lose packets, scramble them, or send them in the wrong order. If your code could handle that, it was good.

sections.title: Specific Test Cases
sections.content:
The RFC lists 13 specific tests that were used to probe for correct behavior. Test 1 opened and closed a single connection many times. Test 2 opened several connections simultaneously, checking that data stayed separated between different connections to the same socket. Test 3 simulated a TCP crash and restart on the same connection. Test 4 used a loop of Telnet connections through multiple TCP instances.

More challenging tests included Test 7 (sending data to a TCP with a zero-sized window), Test 8 (the "Fire Hose" test, opening many connections rapidly), Test 9 (handling urgent data), and Test 11 (sequence number wraparound at 2^31 and 2^32). Test 10, the Kamikaze Segment test, sent specially crafted packets with SYN, EOL, URG, and FIN flags simultaneously to check for crashes.
sections.plainLanguage: Tests tried simple things like opening and closing connections, then harder things like losing connections, sending way too fast, and sending weird packets with every flag turned on at once.

sections.title: New Mechanisms and Performance Tests
sections.content:
The RFC notes that the basic tests check for correct operation and handling of tricky cases, but do not evaluate performance. It suggests new mechanisms that were being developed at the time, including the John Nagel Procedures (RFC 896) for congestion control, the Van Jacobson Procedures involving slow start and round-trip time measurement, and the SQuID Procedures (RFC 1016).

Performance tests described include FTP throughput over Ethernet and ARPANET, NETBLT throughput, and character-echo round-trip time measurement to the Echo Server (RFC 862). These tests were harder to specify because results depended heavily on network conditions, but they provided real-world measurement of TCP/IP efficiency.
sections.plainLanguage: Beyond just checking that things work, people wanted to measure how fast they went. They measured how long it took to send files and get answers back.
